newsitem.title: USA: Some Parkinson's cases genetic in origin.
newsitem.headline: Some Parkinson's cases genetic in origin.

text.p: Scientists have pinpointed genetic markers for Parkinson's Disease, a finding they say establishes that genes play a role in at least some cases of the degenerative nerve disease.

The finding, announced on Thursday by the National Institutes of Health and reported in Friday's edition of the journal Science, comes with many caveats and may or may not bring about any benefits for Parkinson's patients who suffer from tremors, limited mobility and sometimes dementia.

Parkinson's is the second most common neurodegenerative disease after Alzheimer's, afflicting about 1 percent of the population over age 50 or 1 to 1.5 million Americans and millions more around the world. It occurs when nerves in the part of the brain that controls movement degenerate, creating a shortage of a chemical known as dopamine.

Well-known people with Parkinsons include evangelist Billy Graham and U.S. Attorney General Janet Reno. There have also been persistent reports that Parkinson's is the cause of Pope John Paul II's tremor.
Characteristic symptoms include shaking and tremors, rigid muscles, difficulty in moving and dementia. The motor problems can be very limiting and can interfere with speech.
Drugs can control the disease in its early stages and some people can carry out their normal activities for years. But it grows more severe over time and there is no known cure.

"We don't know" when or even if the finding could lead to new therapies or a cure for the progressive disorder, said Zach Hall, head of the National Institute of Neurological Disorders, a branch of NIH.

Other gene discoveries related to degenerative nerve disorders such as Alzheimer's and Huntington's have not yet translated into clinical advances, although they have stimulated new research and theories.

This particular finding, an abnormality along chromosome 4, applies to one vast Italian family, known for reasons of medical privacy as the Contessi kindred for the hometown of a common ancestor 11 generations ago. More than 600 family members have been identified on three continents and about one in 10 are known to have had Parkinson's.

Dr. Mihael Polymeropoulos of the National Center for Human Genome Research and other colleagues have tracked down the region for the gene but have not yet identified or cloned the gene itself. Given the recent advances in gene mapping, that could come relatively quickly.

It is not yet known whether this same gene, as yet undiscovered genes, or perhaps no genes at all play a role in other Parkinson's cases, although the scientists on this research project strongly suspect that genetics will prove a significant component in a disorder that had been commonly attributed to unknown environmental factors.

Dr. Roger Duvoisin, a co-author of the report and a Parkinson's expert from the Robert Wood Johnson Medical School in New Jersey, has long championed the theory that heredity is the key to Parkinson's. He said that from poking around in his patients' family trees for 30 years he has concluded that at the very least a quarter of cases are inherited and his own personal belief is that "all cases are genetic."
